issues.legal_issue: A grant made to a cadet as an appanage ends when the grantee ceases to hold the status of a cadet.
material_facts: The ruler granted a village to his younger son as a Bhayat, for enjoyment as Kapal-Giras and from generation to generation.
The grant and its accompanying statement of rights provided for enjoyment by the grantee and his heirs while a Bhayat survived, and restricted transfer of the grant.
After the elder son and then the ruler died, the younger son was recognised as ruler and ceased to be a Bhayat.
The State treated the grant as lapsed and resumed the village.
issues.conclusion: The grant was made in the grantee’s capacity as a Bhayat and lasted only while he remained a cadet; when he ceased to be a Bhayat, the grant ended and could be resumed.
issues.legal_principle: The grant and the accompanying statement of rights must be read together to determine the nature and duration of the grant. A Bhayat is a cadet or descendant of a younger branch in a family whose estate follows primogeniture. A grant expressly made to a person as a Bhayat for enjoyment as an appanage continues only while the relevant Bhayat status exists; the Court relied on the wording and incidents of the grant, including the succession and transfer terms, and cited no statutory provision or earlier case.

predicates.grant_made_to_grantee_as_cadet_appanage: The grantor gave the property to the grantee in the grantee’s capacity as a cadet and as an appanage.
predicates.grant_lasts_only_while_bhayat_status_exi: The grant’s terms provide for its enjoyment only while a Bhayat status exists.
predicates.grantee_ceases_to_be_bhayat: The grantee ceased to be a cadet of the family.

issues.definition: When a property grant is made to someone as a cadet’s appanage, is limited to the existence of Bhayat status, and the grantee ceases to be a Bhayat, the grant ends.

issues.legal_issue: Resumption of property under a grant that has ended according to its terms does not establish a violation of the grantee’s fundamental rights to that property.
material_facts: The grantee sought relief under Article 32, alleging that State action deprived him of the village granted to him.
The grant was made to him as a Bhayat and ended when he ceased to be a Bhayat after being recognised as ruler.
The State issued a notification treating the grant as lapsed and the village as resumed.
issues.conclusion: Because the grant was defeasible by its nature and had ended when the grantee ceased to be a Bhayat, he failed to establish an infringement of a fundamental right; the petition was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: A claim that State action deprived a person of property depends on the claimant’s rights under the grant. Where the grant, properly construed, ends upon the grantee ceasing to be a Bhayat, resumption after that condition occurs does not establish infringement of a fundamental right. The Court relied on Article 32 as the basis of the petition and on its construction of the grant; it cited no earlier case.

rule.if: constitutional_rights_petition and state_resumes_granted_property and grant_is_defeasible_on_loss_of_cadet_status and grantee_loses_cadet_status

predicates.constitutional_rights_petition: The claimant seeks constitutional relief for an alleged infringement of a fundamental right.
predicates.state_resumes_granted_property: The State resumes property previously granted to the claimant.
predicates.grant_is_defeasible_on_loss_of_cadet_sta: The grant ends under its terms when the grantee ceases to have cadet status.
predicates.grantee_loses_cadet_status: The grantee ceases to have cadet status.

issues.definition: In a constitutional-rights petition, if the State resumes granted property after the grantee loses the status that the grant makes necessary for continued enjoyment, no fundamental-right infringement is established.
